references.text: Moses uses the second half of the blood to sprinkle it on the people and calls it 'the blood of the covenant' - a direct continuation of the blood ritual that begins in verse 6.
The blood from the ram is sprinkled around the altar, the same ritual action that Moses performs with half of the blood in the covenant ceremony.
The priests shall sprinkle the blood around the altar - this is the same ritual practice established in Exodus 24:6.
At peace offerings, the blood is sprinkled around the altar, continuing the ritual tradition of sprinkling blood on the altar.
The priest shall sprinkle the blood on the Lord's altar - the altar as the place for sprinkling blood is central to the sacrificial cult.
The Letter to the Hebrews refers directly to this event and explains how the first covenant was inaugurated with blood, including the sprinkling on the altar and the people.
Jesus' blood is compared to covenant blood - the blood of the new covenant speaks better than Abel's blood, with a clear reference to the covenant blood ritual.
Believers are chosen to be sprinkled with the blood of Jesus Christ - a typological fulfillment of the blood ritual at Sinai.
Both verses illustrate the theological principle that blood must be applied to the altar in order to consecrate or cleanse, even though the context (covenant versus priest) is different.
The verses illuminate each other through the shared ritual logic of applying the blood to people first, before the remainder is used to consecrate the altar.
The direct description of Moses' action of sprinkling the blood on the altar creates a clear ritual connection between the inauguration of the covenant and the inauguration of the priests.
The verse elaborates on the consequence of the blood on the altar by showing how this blood (together with oil) is used to consecrate the ministers.
It confirms that the practice of sprinkling blood on the altar (as in Exodus) was standard for peace offerings also in later times.
